Building a Competitive Intelligence Engine at SAP Concur

Lauren Cochrane led the evaluation and rollout of Crayon and Clozd — creating a centralized competitive intelligence and win-loss system.

By Chris O'Hara · April 15, 2026 · 6 min read

If you want to know what it actually takes to bring new competitive intelligence tools into SAP, Lauren Cochrane has the answers — and the battle scars.

Lauren recently led the evaluation and rollout of two vendors at SAP Concur: Crayon for competitive intelligence and Clozd for win-loss analysis. The result? A centralized competitive intelligence engine that's now being used across sales, marketing, and product teams.

But getting there wasn't easy. When I asked Lauren how the vendor onboarding experience was at SAP, her answer was refreshingly honest: "Not great."

That candor makes her insights even more valuable. For the rest of us looking to bring similar tools into our teams, Lauren's experience is a roadmap — complete with warning signs.

The Tools: Crayon + Clozd

🖍️

Crayon

Competitive Intelligence Platform
Automated tracking, battlecards, and insights delivery. Monitors competitor moves across web, news, reviews, and more.

🎯

Clozd

Win-Loss Analysis
Structured buyer interviews and analysis to understand why deals are won or lost — direct from the decision-makers themselves.

Together, these tools give SAP Concur two complementary views: what competitors are doing (Crayon) and what buyers actually think (Clozd). The combination is powerful — competitive intelligence grounded in real deal outcomes.

What Success Looks Like

Lauren's vision for success is worth quoting in full, because it shows how competitive intelligence should extend beyond just the compete team:

"The Compete and extended product marketing teams use a centralized competitive intelligence engine to efficiently analyze and share insights with stakeholders across the business."
— Lauren Cochrane

But it's the downstream effects that really matter:

💰

Sales Adoption

Greater awareness and proficiency against strategic competitors → higher competitive win rates

📢

Marketing Adoption

Faster iteration on positioning, messaging, and tactics → improved pipeline vs. competitors

🛠️

Product Adoption

Informs product strategy and priorities → keep pace with nimble competitors and differentiate

This is the right way to think about competitive intelligence tools: not as a PMM silo, but as infrastructure that serves the entire go-to-market engine.

The SAP Vendor Reality

Lauren's honest assessment of the onboarding process is a useful heads-up for anyone considering similar tools:

⚠️ Bringing New Vendors into SAP: The Reality

  • Procurement complexity — expect multiple rounds of review
  • Security and compliance — particularly for tools handling competitive data
  • Integration requirements — connecting to existing systems takes time
  • Change management — getting teams to actually adopt new tools

The "not great" experience isn't unique to these vendors — it's the reality of enterprise procurement at scale. What matters is whether the payoff justifies the friction. For Lauren's team, it clearly did.

Lessons for the Broader SAP PMM Community

As we look at rolling out competitive intelligence tools more broadly across SAP, Lauren's experience offers some clear takeaways:

✅ What Worked

  • Two tools, complementary purposes — CI tracking + win-loss analysis gives complete picture
  • Centralized engine approach — one source of truth, multiple consumers
  • Cross-functional adoption goals — designed for sales, marketing, AND product from the start
  • Clear success metrics — tied to win rates, pipeline, and product priorities

The key insight: don't think of competitive intelligence as a tool for the compete team. Think of it as infrastructure for go-to-market excellence.

How Other Teams Can Learn

If you're considering Crayon, Clozd, or similar tools for your team, here's the practical guidance based on Lauren's experience:

  1. Start with the outcome, not the tool — What decisions will this enable? What metrics will improve?
  2. Plan for procurement friction — Build in extra time for security reviews and approvals
  3. Design for multiple stakeholders — Sales, marketing, and product should all see value from day one
  4. Define your "centralized engine" — Where will insights live? How will they flow?
  5. Measure adoption, not just deployment — The tool is only valuable if people use it

The Bigger Picture

Lauren's work at SAP Concur is exactly the kind of operational excellence we need more of across SAP. Rather than relying on ad-hoc competitive research or tribal knowledge locked in individual heads, she's built systematic infrastructure that scales.

That's the shift: from competitive intelligence as occasional project to competitive intelligence as always-on capability.

For those of us thinking about AI tools and automation, this is also a reminder: sometimes the right answer isn't building something custom. It's selecting, evaluating, and implementing best-in-class vendors — then driving adoption across the org.
